title: Mediterranean Hackberry: Ancient Nettle Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: Italians call it spaccasassi, the stone splitter, for roots that crack paving, and plant it in their squares anyway. Sixteen mapped, thirteen cities.
intro: Italians call this tree spaccasassi, the stone splitter, because its roots get into paving and open it, and cities across southern Europe plant it in their squares regardless, because little else gives that much shade on that little water. Celtis australis is deep rooted, drought hardy and indifferent to heat, with a smooth grey trunk closer to a beech than an oak and small dark berries that taste faintly of dates. Mostly it is treated as background, which is why the exceptions stand out. Istanbul protects one by name. Munich registers a group of eight as an extremely rare species, five hundred kilometres north of where the tree grows wild. And a hackberry in Zaragoza came third in Spain's national tree of the year vote in December 2025, put forward by five neighbourhood associations rather than the city. Sixteen are mapped, in thirteen cities, most of them Italian or Spanish.
